title: Service in the rule
hookLine: where and when you'll serve: young Nanak spent his trading money feeding hungry holy men and called it the true bargain
tomorrow: should you love a stranger's baby as much as your own nephew?

cards: Limited time. Best value. Don't miss this deal.
Everyone is selling a good bargain. In the Sikh stories of Guru Nanak's youth, his father, Kalu, wanted one too. He gave his son money and sent him to market with a companion.
Buy something, sell it for more, make a good bargain. Nanak came home with nothing. No goods, no money.
And he told his father he'd made the truest bargain there is.

teach.h: HUNGRY HOLY MEN ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: Here's what happened on the road, as Sikh tradition tells it. Nanak met a group of holy men who were hungry. Not a little hungry.
They had nothing. So he spent all of it on food for them. His father was furious.
That money was supposed to grow. But to Nanak, feeding the hungry was the real profit, the one that doesn't spoil.
Sikhs call the story sacha sauda, the true deal. That's the puzzle solved: the bargain was true because of what it bought. And it seeds a Sikh teaching.
Seva, selfless service, is woven into Sikh life, a duty and a joy at once.
Sikh tradition links this story to langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, where anyone can come in, sit on the floor side by side, and eat the same meal.
Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. Service, in this story, isn't a feeling. It's food, carried to hungry people, at an hour you can name.
For a rule of life, that means writing down where and when you'll serve, so the deal actually gets made.

how: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, and keep langar, the free community kitchen at the gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve and everyone eats together on the floor. A rule of life can name a regular time and place to serve.

games.q: what does “service in the rule” mean?
o: serving yourself first so you have energy for others
a fee paid to a community to become a member
where and when you'll serve others, written into your rule

games.q: the true bargain: tap the pairs.
p: sent Nanak to make a profit
the free kitchen at the gurdwara

s: in the story, Nanak lost the money by accident on the road
he chose to spend it on food for hungry holy men, and called it the true bargain.
at langar, everyone sits together and eats the same meal
anyone can come in, sit side by side on the floor, and eat.
seva is something Sikhs do only when they have free time
in the story and at langar, seva is done at real hours, with real food.

games.q: your friend has a bonus to spend and asks what Nanak's story would say. which fits the true bargain?
o: put part of it toward feeding people who are hungry now.
invest it so there's more to give away someday.
spend it on a nice dinner, since generosity starts with yourself.
games.why: Nanak didn't wait for the money to grow. He fed the hungry in front of him, and called that the true deal.

practice: Name one place you could serve: a kitchen, a shelter, a neighbor, a friend's move. Picture your hands doing the work there: stirring a pot, folding a blanket, carrying one box.
Then let your hands rest in your lap, and sit with the place you named.

wordCard.voice: Service in the rule: where and when you'll serve, written down, like Nanak's true bargain of food for the hungry.

orig.note: Punjabi, Sikh tradition: 'the true deal', the name of Guru Nanak's bargain.

carryVoice: Your line: serve. Nanak's father wanted a profit; Nanak bought a meal for the hungry. See you tomorrow.
